newsitem.title: USA: Reno considers shifting FBI agents for terrorism.
newsitem.headline: Reno considers shifting FBI agents for terrorism.

text.p: The U.S. Justice Department is assessing shifting more FBI agents to fight terrorism and plans to work with the White House and Congress on the issue, Attorney General Janet Reno said on Thursday.

Reno told her weekly news briefing the White House budget office would work with the Justice Department on the proposal that FBI officials said would move as many as 500 agents to investigate domestic and international terrorism.
"The president will be making an announcement, and we will be working with Congress to address this issue," she said.

Justice Department spokesman Bert Brandenburg later said the Clinton administration several months ago sought $18 million from Congress for the 1997 fiscal year to add more than 100 new FBI agents to fight terrorism.
He said it would be "premature" to say the administration had decided on shifting 500 agents, calling it "a work in progress that could change in the future."
Reno said terrorism remained a major threat.
"Since (FBI Director Louis Freeh) and I took office, I have told him that terrorism is, I think, the number-one issue that we have constantly got to be prepared to address," she said.
"I have always suggested to Director Freeh that we must continually assess what our needs are, where the major concerns exist, and be prepared to shift."
Reno and Brandenburg declined to give details on which crime-fighting areas would lose FBI agents as part of the proposed transfers.
FBI officials said earlier the proposal arose after the law enforcement agency found itself stretched thin by a number of high-profile cases and the threat of new terrorist acts.

They said the FBI counter-terrorism unit continued to investigate the June truck bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen in Saudi Arabia, the July 17 crash of TWA Flight 800 that killed 230 people and the July 27 bombing at the Olympics park in Atlanta that killed two people and injured 111.
Reno warned reporters not to conclude that the evidence so far points to a bomb as having caused the explosion of the Paris-bound TWA airliner shortly after takeoff in New York.
"I would urge you not to jump to conclusions about what the evidence suggests," she said.

Aside from a bomb, investigators are looking into whether the plane was brought down by a missile or mechanical failure. Reno said investigators were still considering "all the possibilities" and could not say whether a criminal act caused the crash.
